title: Can I Get Pregnant With PCOS?
seoTitle: Can I get pregnant with PCOS or PMOS?
description: Many people with PCOS/PMOS conceive, with or without help. See ovulation checks, partner factors, treatment categories, and earlier referral timing.
primaryQuestion: Can I get pregnant with PCOS?
directAnswer: Yes. Many people with PCOS/PMOS conceive, some without fertility treatment and some with carefully chosen medical help. Irregular or infrequent ovulation is often the main barrier, but the diagnosis alone does not make pregnancy impossible. Age, other pelvic factors, semen findings, metabolic health and medicines all shape the plan, so no article can promise your personal outcome.

sections.heading: What usually gets in the way, and what does not
paragraphs: For fertility, the central issue is often how predictably you release an egg. Some people with PCOS/PMOS still ovulate most months; others go long stretches without a clear ovulatory bleed. Body size, acne or an ultrasound description of “polycystic ovaries” should not be treated as a verdict on whether pregnancy can occur.

Possibility and probability are different ideas. Education can explain the first; only assessment and time can clarify the second for you. Avoid both extremes of messaging: neither “you will never conceive” nor “treatment always works” is honest clinical care. Our what-is-PCOS guide explains the condition itself.
If bleeds look regular on hormonal contraception, that calendar still may not reflect natural ovulation. Say what method you use and when you stopped it when you start trying.

sections.heading: The usual pathway: ovulation and other fertility factors
paragraphs: Cycle length and bleeding pattern are the starting story. Very long gaps, absent periods, or bleeds that appear only after medicines suggest ovulation may be infrequent. Tracking ovulation with bleed dates, mucus notes or urine kits can support the conversation, but kits may show confusing positives in PCOS/PMOS and do not clear the tubes or assess semen.

Other fertility factors belong early, not after months focused only on the ovaries. ASRM’s 2026 fertility-evaluation opinion emphasises evaluating both partners in a systematic way, including at least one semen analysis, because male factor contributes in a large share of couples. Tubal or uterine history (past infection, surgery, endometriosis symptoms) can change imaging timing even when anovulation seems obvious.

Ask what each suggested step is meant to answer. “Will this tell us if I ovulate?” is a different question from “Should we check tubes before starting ovulation induction?” Clarity reduces the sense that every form is an automatic leap toward IVF.

sections.heading: Preconception care and treatment categories
paragraphs: Before active fertility treatment, routine preconception care still matters: review medicines, vaccinations where relevant, smoking and alcohol, blood pressure and glucose risk, and start folic acid as discussed in our folic-acid-before-pregnancy guide. The 2023 international PCOS/PMOS guideline also frames prenatal vitamin supplementation and optimisation of preconception risk factors as part of fertility care.

Support then falls into broad categories rather than a single protocol. Lifestyle and metabolic review may sit alongside cycle monitoring. Some people need help inducing ovulation; others need tubal imaging, treatment of a concurrent condition, intrauterine insemination, or IVF when findings and goals point that way.

For anovulatory infertility in PCOS/PMOS with no other infertility factors, the 2023 international guideline recommends letrozole as first-line pharmacological ovulation induction. The same guideline notes that ovulation-induction agents, including letrozole, remain off-label in many countries and that clinicians should explain evidence, concerns and side effects where use is allowed. Whether it suits you, and at what dose, is decided by your gynaecologist after assessment and monitoring.

sections.heading: When to seek fertility help without waiting a full year
paragraphs: ASRM’s 2026 committee opinion commonly organises evaluation around about twelve months of trying if the female partner is under 35, about six months from 35, and sooner after 40. It also advises not delaying when a condition known to impair fertility is already present. Irregular cycles (ASRM cites cycles shorter than 25 or longer than 35 days), amenorrhoea, intermenstrual bleeding, known or suspected tubal disease or endometriosis, and known or suspected male subfertility are among the reasons for earlier assessment.

In practical terms, irregular or absent periods often mean you should not wait for a twelve-month calendar milestone before asking for a fertility-focused visit. Our when-to-see-a-fertility-specialist guide explains referral timing in more depth.

If you have been told to address weight, thyroid imbalance or endometriosis pain first, ask for a review date so those steps stay connected to your fertility timeline rather than becoming an indefinite delay.

sections.heading: Urgent symptoms while trying to conceive
paragraphs: After a positive pregnancy test, go straight to emergency care for knife-like pain on one side of the pelvis, pain into the shoulder tip, blackouts, or soaking haemorrhage. NHS ectopic-pregnancy pages also urge prompt review for concerning symptom clusters if pregnancy is possible before a test turns positive, and emergency help when abrupt severe abdominal pain arrives with dizziness.
Those crises sit outside PCOS education and outside routine fertility messaging. Resume ovulation planning only after acute care is complete.

Ordinary bookings with Dr. Charmi Shah remain the right door for cycle strategy, ovulation questions, preconception counselling and stepwise fertility evaluation, without promising any individual pregnancy result.

faqs.question: Do regular-looking periods mean I am ovulating with PCOS/PMOS?
faqs.answer: Not always. Some people bleed on a predictable schedule yet ovulate infrequently, and hormonal contraception can create scheduled bleeds that are not natural cycles. Ask how ovulation will be assessed in your situation rather than relying on the calendar alone.

faqs.question: Should my partner be tested if I have PCOS/PMOS?
faqs.answer: Yes, when pregnancy involves sperm. ASRM advises evaluating both partners and including semen analysis early so months are not spent focusing only on ovarian factors while a male factor goes unnoticed.
